      "piece_id": "01",
      "markdown": "# Beyond code generation: remote control, security review and runtime inspection

*As of 2026-10-15*

Recent AI coding developments are worth examining for what they add around implementation, rather than treating them as proof that software now finishes itself. Cursor has announced remote interaction with local agents and repository-enabled security review. Simon Willison reports using Codex to inspect an application's execution. Alongside those developments, GitHub has explained an incident in which code-review jobs reported success without delivering reviews. Together, these sources support an output-focused question: what inspectable result did the assistant actually leave behind? [01-c5]

## Remote supervision is still local execution

Cursor's October 6 announcement says its iOS app can display local agents running on a developer's computer and let the developer message them. The distinction is important: this is remote interaction, not a transfer of execution to the cloud. Cursor explicitly says the agent continues running on the computer, which must remain on and online. ([Cursor, “Remote control for local agents,” 2026-10-06](https://cursor.com/changelog/remote-control-local-agents).) [01-c1]

For an individual developer, the capability to investigate is therefore supervision away from the keyboard. It does not, on the supplied evidence, remove dependence on the original machine or demonstrate that the agent needs less supervision. Being able to see what an agent is doing and send another message broadens the interface to the work; it does not establish that the work is correct. That is an interpretation of the announced control, not a measured outcome from using it. [01-c1] [01-c5]

## A review format, with access restrictions

Cursor's September 23 Security Review announcement describes enabling review for selected repositories. Each finding is supposed to include a severity, an attack path and a proposed fix. An attack path is the account of how the reported problem could be reached or exploited. Draft pull requests—proposed changes still marked as drafts—are skipped, and the announcement offers access on Teams and Enterprise plans. ([Cursor, “Rollouts and Security Review,” 2026-09-23](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer).) [01-c2]

Those details establish an announced output format and boundaries, not detection effectiveness. For someone building a small project alone, access is part of the evaluation: the announcement does not resolve whether purchasing an eligible plan is practical. Nor does a structured finding establish that the alleged vulnerability exists or that its proposed repair is correct. The useful development is a review output that can be inspected, rather than evidence that security checking has been settled. [01-c2] [01-c5]

## Inspecting execution, not demonstrating a speedup

Willison's October 12 account provides a different kind of example. He reports having Codex run Python 3.15's profiler against his web-edit application, producing an example flame graph and heatmap—visual profiling outputs for inspecting execution. This is a concrete account of an assistant helping investigate running software, rather than only generating an implementation. ([Simon Willison, “Profiling web-edit with Python 3.15,” 2026-10-12](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/).) [01-c3]

The boundary matters. The account demonstrates neither a completed optimization nor a measured saving in delivery time. It is also an experienced maintainer's report about his own application, without a controlled comparison or complete accounting of testing and correction effort. A developer with basic skills may still need additional setup and interpretation; the example does not establish reproducibility for that audience. [01-c3]

## “Completed” was not “delivered”

GitHub's availability report, published October 14, supplies a counterweight. Explaining its September 28 Copilot code-review incident, GitHub says some jobs could not build a review but nevertheless reported successful completion. It says missing review results were not detected because monitoring was lacking. GitHub reports reverting the change and advising customers to request affected reviews again. ([GitHub, “GitHub availability report: September 2026,” published 2026-10-14; incident section: September 28, 21:16 UTC](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/).) [01-c4]

This is GitHub's own account of its incident and mitigation, not an independent reliability assessment. It nevertheless makes the distinction between a completion signal and a delivered result explicit. [01-c4]

The combined implication is modest: judge these developments by actual agent changes, a delivered review or a runtime profile. Cursor and GitHub describe products they sell; Willison supplies a first-person example. These sources do not provide independent evidence of solo-project completion gains, representative beginner outcomes or the experience of abandoned projects and accessibility users. Broader development actions are worth investigating, but finishing still needs an inspectable result—not merely an agent saying it is done. [01-c5]",

      "piece_id": "02",
      "markdown": "# Review activity is not the same as verified correctness

*As of 2026-10-15*

An AI review can produce criticism, prompt an edit or suggest a repair. Those are different outcomes from confirming a defect and establishing that the repair is correct. The current evidence spans a benchmark, a product announcement and a practitioner's experimental habit. Each illuminates part of review, but their combination does not close the gap between receiving criticism and delivering correct software. For a small project, the defensible interpretation is to treat AI criticism as a candidate finding until its relevance and behavior have been checked. [02-c5]

## Ask which changes a benchmark represents

GitHub describes ReviewBench as containing 219 pull requests from 187 public open-source-licensed repositories across 19 languages. It says language and repository-size distributions closely match GitHub overall, but identifies a deliberate adjustment: reducing the representation of tiny, single-file changes in favor of more substantive, multi-file reviews. ([GitHub, “ReviewBench: An open benchmark for AI code review,” 2026-10-05](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/).) [02-c1]

That makes task selection part of interpreting results. A developer considering assistance with a tiny solo-project edit should not assume that matching the benchmark's language is enough to establish relevance. The source itself says change size was reweighted. This is not a reason to dismiss ReviewBench; it is a reason to ask how closely its review tasks resemble the change under consideration. [02-c1]

## A response metric is not a correctness check

GitHub defines “addressed rate,” its online counterpart to precision, as the percentage of Copilot code-review comments that an LLM judges prompted a corresponding code change. The judgment draws on the diff, discussion thread, reactions, resolution state and post-review code. In plain terms, the metric estimates whether developers acted on comments. It does not independently establish that those comments identified real defects or that subsequent edits removed them. ([GitHub, “ReviewBench,” 2026-10-05](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/).) [02-c2]

GitHub also acknowledges a separate measurement limitation: a fixed “golden set,” or expected list of findings, becomes incomplete as systems discover issues its creators did not anticipate. That creates a genuine tension. Scoring only expected findings may overlook useful discoveries, while measuring a developer's response still leaves correctness unresolved. Neither limitation makes evaluation pointless; both limit what a score can support. [02-c2]

## A second critic remains a critic

Willison reports trying adversarial review in his own projects: asking a model to find flaws and sometimes playing Claude and GPT against each other. His October 13 account establishes that he is experimenting with this practice. It does not supply a measured improvement in defect detection, a review-cost comparison or artifacts establishing the outcome of those reviews. ([Simon Willison, “Redesigning source control at Anthropic,” 2026-10-13](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/redesigning-source-control-at-anthropic/).) [02-c3]

The practice is relevant as a way to request criticism, not as independent confirmation that the criticism is right. An experienced practitioner's willingness to try a second reviewer should not be converted into evidence that a beginner will obtain more reliable software from the same arrangement. That transfer remains unestablished here. [02-c3] [02-c5]

## Actionable fields are not detection results

Cursor says Security Review looks for injection across SQL, command and template surfaces, plus authentication and authorization bypasses, including checks that stopped running after a refactor. It promises findings with severity, an attack path and a proposed fix. These are advertised targets and output fields—not an evaluation of how many real vulnerabilities the system finds or misses. ([Cursor, “Rollouts and Security Review,” 2026-09-23](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer).) [02-c4]

An attack path can make an allegation more concrete, but a concrete allegation remains something to verify. A researcher interviewed by GitHub puts the principle directly: “The main thing I’d say is to always verify what the AI gives you and never submit a finding you haven’t confirmed yourself.” ([GitHub, bug-bounty researcher interview, 2026-10-08](https://github.blog/security/how-one-bug-bounty-researcher-chooses-the-features-they-investigate/).) [02-c5]

The synthesis is therefore a separation, not a ranking. ReviewBench concerns evaluation and inferred response; Willison describes a review habit; Cursor specifies promised findings. GitHub and Cursor also have commercial interests in the tools they discuss. None of these sources alone demonstrates a confirmed defect followed by a correct repair, and none supplies representative first-time-user or unsuccessful-project outcomes. The acceptance criterion should remain checked behavior, not review activity. [02-c5]",

      "piece_id": "03",
      "markdown": "# Try one bounded task—and account for the work needed to verify it

*As of 2026-10-15*

For an individual developer, the defensible next step is a small, reversible trial—not immediate adoption of a more elaborate agent workflow. Define what would count as success, inspect the delivered evidence and record the effort required to reach an acceptable result. This is a proposed evaluation approach, not a workflow tested here or a claim that one task size is best. The aim is to measure verified delivery cost rather than generation alone. [03-c5]

## Start with one convention

GitHub's beginner tutorial recommends adding repository guidance in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, including conventions and expectations for testing and validation. Its closing advice is deliberately incremental: choose one convention repeatedly explained to Copilot and see how it applies that guidance to the next task. ([GitHub, “How to teach Copilot about your codebase,” 2026-10-12](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/github-copilot-app-for-beginners-how-to-teach-copilot-about-your-codebase/).) [03-c1]

A bounded trial could therefore begin with one convention and explicit validation commands, rather than every available customization. Inspect whether the resulting change follows the instruction and whether the requested validation actually happened. The file communicates guidance; it should not be treated as an enforced guarantee. Keeping the trial narrow makes that particular question the object of evaluation, without claiming that the setup will improve every subsequent task. [03-c1]

## Check what a profile actually observed

Verification setup deserves attention of its own. In Willison's web-edit profiling report, 95.1% of recorded stacks came from AnyIO's worker thread. He says a main-thread-only profile would have missed them. His accompanying Python article explains sampling as periodically capturing stack traces from running processes to estimate where execution time is spent. ([Simon Willison, web-edit profiling report, 2026-10-12](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/); [Python 3.15 overview, 2026-10-12](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15/).) [03-c2]

The proposed check for an assistant's Python performance suggestion is consequently specific: reproduce a relevant workload, include the threads doing the work and then compare the proposed change. A profile's sample frequencies alone do not demonstrate elapsed-time savings. Also check setup requirements rather than copying an example blindly: Willison reports needing `sudo` on macOS to attach the profiler. His result motivates inspecting coverage; it does not establish that another application's useful profile will have the same configuration. [03-c2]

## Make security review a conditional trial

Cursor's announcement offers Security Review on Teams and Enterprise plans, with findings containing severity, an attack path and a proposed fix. Check current access and price before planning a trial around it. On an authorized test copy, the proposed evaluation is to reproduce the reported behavior using the attack path, then check whether the fix removes that behavior without breaking intended use. ([Cursor, “Rollouts and Security Review,” 2026-09-23](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer).) [03-c3]

This is not an adoption recommendation. It follows the verification principle expressed by a researcher in GitHub's October 8 interview: never submit an AI finding without confirming it yourself. Access to a reviewer and receipt of a proposed fix are starting conditions for this check, not substitutes for it. ([GitHub, bug-bounty researcher interview, 2026-10-08](https://github.blog/security/how-one-bug-bounty-researcher-chooses-the-features-they-investigate/).) [03-c3]

## Budget for the whole attempt

The HTML All The Things hosts describe contrasting usage experiences. One reports mostly short tasks and no further limit after switching back to another model. The other describes combining shorter steps into longer workflows and exhausting usage. These are attributed experiences, not a controlled comparison or evidence of model superiority. ([HTML All The Things, “AI’s Biggest Problem Isn’t Intelligence Anymore,” 2026-09-26, 04:20–04:44, segments s00076, s00078, s00081; 07:17–07:36, segments s00131, s00132, s00136](https://www.htmlallthethings.com/podcast/ais-biggest-problem-isnt-intelligence-anymore).) [03-c4]

For the next trial, record acceptance checks, delivered outputs, retries, quota use or API spending, and human testing and correction time. Willison's pricing discussion reinforces why a unit price is insufficient: his stated concern is how many tokens a model needs to achieve a goal within an agent workflow. ([Simon Willison, “llm-gemini 0.35,” 2026-10-13](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/llm-gemini/).) [03-c5]

Expand only after reviewing that record. Beginners may need substantial verification setup, especially without a useful test suite; experienced practitioners' accounts do not settle that cost. Eligibility, compatibility, permissions, quotas and prices remain checks to perform. None of this evidence proves that another reviewer or paid tool will repay its setup effort. The useful next result is a bounded task whose output and total verification burden you can inspect. [03-c5]",
